Oh man am I glad you asked. This is a HUGE topic but I'll try to cut it down as much as possible.

The biggest problem today in the agriculture industry is the rise of the corporate farmer. These guys produce most of the food that gets into the grocery stores today and they make up roughly 80% of the industry nation wide. They also consume 26.28 billion dollars a year through farming subsidies (roughly 3% of our national spending). This has created a whole host of problems for the small farmers. These problems include, but are not limited too, the emptying of water aquifers, the rise of herbicide resistant weeds and bugs and bee decline nation wide.

In a normal supply/demand market producing acres would be maybe a fifth of what they are today. But because the government has continued to pay these corporate farmers year after year we continue to produce like there's a massive food shortage. The opposite in fact is true. Our nation now stockpiles a RIDICULOUS amount of Corn, Cotton and Wheat (this point is touched on in 'Food Inc.'). I've heard estimates before that say that we could go without the production of these commodities for as much as six years before demand would rise for them again.

Farming subsidies were started in the FDR era to bail out farmers who were leaving they're homes in the 30's due to the dust bowl. People like my great grandparents got to keep they're land due to the governments checks. By the time the economy recovered, world war 2 was on it's way and the government began increasing the subsidies to farmers in order to fund the war effort. After the war we continued to pay our farmers through the various recessions between then and now. The argument that is commonly made for this is that "Americans should have access to the cheapest commodities in the world". Today, the farming industry is basically on life support. No farmer could make money in the industry without receiving at least 30% of his income from the government.

Here's where the problem comes in. The size of these checks is dependent upon the amount of acres producing and not financial need. So, the corporate farmer produces ALOT of corn, cotton and wheat and in exchange pockets a huge check from uncle sam. Then he turns around and sells his produce for next to nothing (making the market even more flooded). The corporate farmer uses tons of artificial nitrogen and noxious herbicides to maximize his production and minimize the amount of labor needed. He uses the latest in genetic modification to control pests and maximize yields. He pumps what little water is left out of the aquifers to grow acres upon acres of crops that will probably never be consumed.

So, what is the solution you ask? Well, I suppose we could probably enforce stronger regulations on herbicide application. But, the guys enforcing it will probably be bought by the lobbyists or maybe the chemical manufacturers come up with an even worse chemical for controlling these problems. Ultimately though, this is just putting a band aid on a severed limb.

What needs to happen is a massive slashing of the governments subsidies to farmers. Me saying this is possibly career suicide if people in the industry found out. I have friends who were completely cut out of the industry for saying this same thing. But it has to be said. We need to speak out, or else this will never end.
